I'm a 31-year-old farmer in Quzhou County with four years under my belt. Four years is enough to know that this land rewards discipline but punishes waste. I've got 225 mu, which is a sizable holding for this area, and a household of four that depends on it. My well gives me reliable water, and I intend to use that advantage strategically.

I've decided to put 150 mu into my wheat-maize double-cropping system and keep 75 mu in cotton. The wheat-maize rotation is the backbone—it's stable, the machinery and buyers are here in Handan, and with irrigation I can push yields consistently. Cotton is a cash crop risk; prices swing, but 75 mu gives me diversification without overexposure.

For the winter wheat already in the ground, I'm using an improved variety. With my well, I'll irrigate three times: the green-up water, the jointing stage, and one at grain filling. I'll top-dress nitrogen accordingly and keep pesticides minimal—two applications, herbicide early and one fungicide if the weather turns humid. I'll rotary-till after harvest to prepare for maize.

Summer maize has to go in fast after wheat harvest, so I'm going no-tillage with a hybrid seed to save time and preserve soil moisture. Two irrigations and two pesticide sprays are enough if I stay on top of it.

For cotton, I'm planting a hybrid Bt variety in spring. Cotton is hungry for potassium, so I'll push the potash higher. Three irrigations at seedling, flowering, and boll stages, and three pesticide rounds—Bt handles the bollworm, but I still watch for aphids and mites.

My education tells me that balanced fertilizer beats throwing extra nitrogen at problems. My four years of experience tell me not to bet everything on one crop.
